title: How to Program an AI Assistant: Step-by-Step 2026 Guide
description: Program an AI assistant from scratch: pick a free LLM API, add a system prompt, memory, tool calling, retrieval, and guardrails in Python.
author: freellm.site
content:
Programming an AI assistant means connecting four things: a language model you call over an API, a system prompt that defines its behaviour, a conversation history you resend on every turn, and a set of tools (plain functions) the model is allowed to call. You don't train a model yourself. You rent one through an API, and the assistant is the Python (or JavaScript) loop you write around it.

Below is the whole build, in order, with runnable code. Every provider named here has a free tier, so you can follow along without a credit card.

![How to Program an AI Assistant: Step-by-Step 2026 Guide](/images/blog/program-an-ai-assistant-guide/image-0.jpg)

## The three parts of any AI assistant

Every assistant, whether it's ChatGPT, Claude Code, a support bot or your weekend side project, has the same three layers:

1. **The model.** A hosted LLM that takes a list of messages and returns the next message. You don't build this part.
2. **The context you send it.** The system prompt, the conversation history and any retrieved documents. This decides most of the quality.
3. **The loop around it.** Code that reads user input, calls the model, runs any tool the model asked for, feeds the result back, and decides when to stop.

The most important fact: the model is stateless. It remembers nothing between calls, so every request has to carry the entire conversation. That's why context windows and token budgets start to matter as soon as people use your assistant for real.

## Step 1: Pick a model and get a key

Start with whichever free tier has the limits and latency you need, and switch later if you have to. Almost all of these use the same request format, so switching is a two-line change; [what an OpenAI-compatible API is](/blog/openai-compatible-api-guide/) explains why.

| Provider | Good for | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| [Groq](/providers/groq/) | Fast, chatty assistants | Very low latency; open-weight models |
| [Google Gemini](/providers/google_gemini/) | Long documents, multimodal | Large context window on the free tier |
| [Mistral](/providers/mistral/) | Tool calling, European hosting | Clean function-calling support |
| [Cerebras](/providers/cerebras/) | Throughput-heavy loops | Speed-focused inference |
| [OpenRouter](/providers/openrouter/) | Trying many models behind one key | One endpoint, many vendors |
| [Hugging Face](/providers/huggingface/) | Open models, experimentation | Wide model selection |

Rate limits, context sizes and model names change often, so check each provider's official docs for exact figures; I'm not going to quote numbers that may be stale by the time you read this. For the current options, start with [the best free LLM APIs in 2026](/blog/best-free-llm-apis-2026/) and [free LLM API rate limits compared](/blog/free-llm-api-rate-limits-compared/).

Set your key as an environment variable. Never paste it into source code, and never into a frontend bundle:

```bash
export LLM_API_KEY=your_key_here
```

## Step 2: The smallest assistant that works

Install the OpenAI SDK. It's the de facto client for OpenAI-compatible endpoints, which most free providers offer.

```bash
pip install openai
```

```python
import os
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    api_key=os.environ['LLM_API_KEY'],
    base_url='https://api.groq.com/openai/v1',  # swap for your provider
)

resp = client.chat.completions.create(
    model='llama-3.3-70b-versatile',  # check your provider docs for valid IDs
    messages=[
        {'role': 'system', 'content': 'You are a terse assistant. Answer in under 3 sentences.'},
        {'role': 'user', 'content': 'What is a vector database?'},
    ],
)

print(resp.choices[0].message.content)
```

That's a working assistant. It has no memory and no tools, but you'll use this same request shape for everything else.

## Step 3: Write a system prompt that constrains behaviour

The system prompt is the cheapest and most effective control you have. A vague prompt gives you a vague assistant. A usable one specifies role, scope, tone, refusal policy and output format:

```python
SYSTEM = '''You are Ada, a support assistant for Acme Hosting.

Scope: billing, DNS, and uptime questions only.
If asked anything outside that, say so and offer to open a ticket.

Style: direct, no apologies, max 120 words.
Never invent prices, SLAs, or refund policy. If you are unsure, say you are unsure
and recommend the customer check the billing page.

Always end with one concrete next step.'''
```

Two things to keep in mind. Over a long conversation, models drift toward the user's voice, the effect described in [why ChatGPT sounds like you](/blog/why-chatgpt-sounds-like-you/), and a firm style instruction in the system prompt is your main defence. And every model behaves differently under pressure; if you're choosing between them, [what it feels like to use Claude](/blog/what-it-feels-like-to-use-claude/) and [why Gemini sounds stressed](/blog/why-gemini-sounds-stressed-panic-replies/) both cover this.

## Step 4: Add memory

Memory is a list you keep appending to and resending:

```python
class Assistant:
    def __init__(self, client, model, system):
        self.client = client
        self.model = model
        self.history = [{'role': 'system', 'content': system}]

    def say(self, text):
        self.history.append({'role': 'user', 'content': text})
        resp = self.client.chat.completions.create(
            model=self.model,
            messages=self.history,
        )
        msg = resp.choices[0].message
        self.history.append({'role': 'assistant', 'content': msg.content})
        return msg.content

bot = Assistant(client, 'llama-3.3-70b-versatile', SYSTEM)
print(bot.say('My DNS is not resolving.'))
print(bot.say('I already tried that.'))  # it remembers, because you resent everything
```

That list grows without limit, and every extra message costs tokens and money. Three standard fixes:

- **Window.** Keep the system message plus the last N turns.
- **Summarise.** When the history passes a threshold, ask the model to compress the older turns into a short summary message and keep that instead.
- **Externalise.** Store facts (name, plan, open tickets) in a database and inject only the relevant ones.

If your assistant really needs a lot of raw context instead of summaries, choose a model with a big window; see [free LLM APIs with the largest context windows](/blog/free-llm-api-largest-context-window/).

## Step 5: Give it tools (function calling)

Tools are what turn a chatbot into an assistant. You describe your Python functions as JSON schemas, the model decides when it needs one and returns a structured call, you run it, and you hand the result back.

```python
import json

def get_order_status(order_id: str) -> dict:
    # real code: hit your own database or API
    return {'order_id': order_id, 'status': 'shipped', 'eta_days': 2}

TOOLS = [{
    'type': 'function',
    'function': {
        'name': 'get_order_status',
        'description': 'Look up the shipping status of a customer order.',
        'parameters': {
            'type': 'object',
            'properties': {
                'order_id': {'type': 'string', 'description': 'The order ID, e.g. A-1042'},
            },
            'required': ['order_id'],
        },
    },
}]

REGISTRY = {'get_order_status': get_order_status}

def run(messages, model, max_steps=5):
    for _ in range(max_steps):
        resp = client.chat.completions.create(
            model=model, messages=messages, tools=TOOLS,
        )
        msg = resp.choices[0].message
        messages.append(msg.model_dump(exclude_none=True))

        if not msg.tool_calls:
            return msg.content

        for call in msg.tool_calls:
            fn = REGISTRY[call.function.name]
            args = json.loads(call.function.arguments)
            result = fn(**args)
            messages.append({
                'role': 'tool',
                'tool_call_id': call.id,
                'content': json.dumps(result),
            })
    return 'Stopped: too many tool steps.'

msgs = [
    {'role': 'system', 'content': SYSTEM},
    {'role': 'user', 'content': 'Where is order A-1042?'},
]
print(run(msgs, 'llama-3.3-70b-versatile'))
```

Notes that will save you hours:

- You need the `max_steps` cap, because models loop. Agent loops that can't end are a known failure, covered in [why two AI agents cannot end a conversation](/blog/ai-agents-cant-end-conversations/).
- Tool arguments are model output, so they're **untrusted input**. Validate `order_id` against a pattern before it touches your database. Never pass model-generated strings into shell commands, SQL concatenation, or file paths.
- Tool descriptions are part of the prompt. A vague description is the most common reason a model picks the wrong tool.
- The schema format differs slightly between vendors. The canonical references are the [OpenAI function-calling docs](https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/function-calling), the [Google Gemini function-calling docs](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/function-calling), the [Mistral function-calling docs](https://docs.mistral.ai/capabilities/function_calling/), and the [Groq tool-use docs](https://console.groq.com/docs/tool-use).

## Step 6: Let it answer from your own documents

For anything specific to your company or project, retrieve before you consider fine-tuning. Embed your docs, store the vectors, and for each question fetch the top few chunks and paste them into the prompt, with an instruction to answer only from that context and to say so when the answer isn't there.

That pattern, retrieval-augmented generation, is what separates an assistant that confidently makes things up from one that cites your handbook. Setup details, including which free tiers offer embeddings, are in [the best free LLM API for RAG](/blog/free-llm-api-for-rag-embeddings/).

## Step 7: Guardrails, then ship

Before anyone else uses it:

- **Cap spend and turns.** Set per-user rate limits, a max token budget per conversation, and a hard step limit in the tool loop.
- **Handle failure visibly.** Wrap every API call in try/except with retry and backoff. 429s and timeouts are normal.
- **Keep the key server-side.** The model call happens on your backend, and the browser never sees the key.
- **Log prompts and tool calls.** You can't debug an assistant you can't replay.
- **Decide what it must refuse** and put that in the system prompt plus a check in code. Refusing too much is a bug too, as [the Granny Benchmark](/blog/claude-granny-benchmark-bieber-lyrics/) shows.
- **Know who is responsible when it acts.** If your assistant can send email, issue refunds or change records, read [who is liable when an AI agent breaks the law](/blog/who-is-liable-when-ai-agents-break-the-law/) and the [FTC position on developer liability](/blog/ftc-ai-agent-liability-developers/) before you let it loose.

To deploy, a Discord or Telegram bot is the fastest way to get real users and real feedback: [build one with a free LLM API](/blog/free-llm-api-discord-telegram-bot/).

## Which build path should you take?

| Path | Effort | You control | Best when |
|---|---|---|---|
| Raw API + your own loop | Low to medium | Everything | You want to understand the system; small, specific assistants |
| Framework (agent library) | Medium | Most things | Many tools, multi-step planning, you want retries and tracing included |
| Hosted assistant platform | Low | Little | Prototype or demo, no infrastructure appetite |
| Local model on your machine | High | All of it, plus data | Privacy requirements or offline use |

Start with the raw API. Frameworks hide the loop, and you need to understand the loop to debug anything. Once you know why the model asked for the wrong tool, a framework saves you work instead of hiding the problem.

Coding assistants aren't free productivity either. Read the [Harvard study on Claude Code productivity gains](/blog/harvard-claude-code-productivity-study/) before you promise your team a speedup you can't measure.

## Common mistakes

- **Forgetting the model is stateless.** If it doesn't remember, you didn't resend the history.
- **Stuffing everything into the system prompt.** Retrieve instead; a long static prompt costs tokens on every turn.
- **Trusting tool arguments.** Validate them like any other user input.
- **No step limit.** Expect loops.
- **Picking the biggest model by default.** Most assistant work is routing, extraction and summarising, where a smaller fast model is often better and cheaper. Token efficiency matters too; see the [Particle-1 token-efficiency guide](/blog/particle-ai-particle-1-guide/).

## FAQ

### Do I need to train my own model to build an AI assistant?

No. You call a hosted model over an API and write the logic around it. Consider training or fine-tuning only after prompting plus retrieval has clearly failed, which happens less often than people expect.

### What language should I program an AI assistant in?

Python has the most mature SDKs and retrieval tooling, and JavaScript/TypeScript is the natural choice if the assistant lives in a web app. Both are well supported, and any language that can make an HTTPS request will work.

### How much does it cost to run?

You can prototype for free on the tiers listed above. Costs start once you have steady traffic, and they scale with tokens, which means with conversation length. For current per-token prices, check the provider's own pricing page, then compare with [the cheapest LLM API after the free tier](/blog/cheapest-llm-api-after-free-tier/).

### How do I stop my assistant from making things up?

Ground it. Retrieve real documents, tell it to answer only from the supplied context, give it tools to look up live facts, and have it say it doesn't know instead of guessing. Hallucination is partly a design problem; [this account of a Gemini hallucination](/blog/gemini-hallucinated-notification-grief/) shows how badly a confident wrong answer can land.

### Can one assistant use several models at once?

Yes, and it's often the right design: a small fast model for classification and routing, and a larger one for hard reasoning. [How Grok's multi-agent mode works](/blog/grok-4-20-multi-agent-guide/) is a useful example of a multi-model setup. A gateway like [OpenRouter](/providers/openrouter/) makes switching between models easy.
